findings.title: REQUIREMENT_PATTERN can fail to match, so Requirement() raises AttributeError instead of VersionError — one bad manifest aborts the entire scan
findings.failing_input:
Any requirement string containing an embedded newline followed by more non-whitespace text, e.g. a mod.json with `"dependencies": [{"mod_id": "alphamod", "version": "1.0.0
WHATEVER"}]` (also reachable via `"framework_api": "^0.4.0
x"` or a `conflicts[].version`). REQUIREMENT_PATTERN = `^(==|>=|\^)?\s*(.+)$` (semver.py:31): `.` does not match `
` and `$` only matches before a newline that is the LAST character, so `re.match` returns None. Line 96 then does `match.group(1)` on None. Verified: `semver.Requirement('1.0.0
x')` -> AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'group'. Note `text.strip()` at line 94 cannot remove an interior newline, and `Version()` is not affected because it checks `if not match` at line 48.
findings.why_it_matters: manifest.py catches only `semver.VersionError` (lines 234-239, 282-287, 411-414, 418-421), so the AttributeError escapes parse() -> load() -> discovery.discover() -> resolve.plan_from_root() as an uncaught traceback. Confirmed against a two-mod root: the pipeline died at manifest.py:234 with no diagnostic, no LoadPlan, and the healthy `alphamod` in the sibling folder was never discovered either. This violates "must detect malformed manifest" and the fail-closed-per-mod contract: instead of excluding the one offending mod with a MALFORMED_MANIFEST diagnostic, a single mod author can crash discovery for every mod in the install with a two-character JSON edit.

findings.title: A dependency entry with no "version" key defaults to "0.0.0", which means ^0.0.0 (major must be 0) and wrongly excludes any dependency at 1.x or later
findings.failing_input: Two valid mods: alphamod at version 1.0.0, and betamod declaring `"dependencies": [{"mod_id": "alphamod"}]` with the optional `version` key omitted (this is accepted — `_dependency_list` only rejects keys outside {mod_id, version}). `entry.get("version", "0.0.0")` yields `Requirement("0.0.0")`, whose operator defaults to `^` (semver.py:96), so `matches()` at semver.py:123-124 requires `version.major == 0`. Verified end-to-end: plan.load_order == ['alphamod'], plan.excluded == {'betamod': ['incompatible_dependency_version']}, diagnostic detail "requires 'alphamod' 0.0.0 but the installed 'alphamod' is 1.0.0".
findings.why_it_matters: The sentinel `"0.0.0"` is clearly meant as "no constraint" (it is the lowest possible version), but the caret default silently turns it into "must be a 0.x release". Any mod that omits the version key on a dependency is excluded with a false INCOMPATIBLE_DEPENDENCY_VERSION the moment its dependency reaches 1.0.0, and that exclusion then propagates to every dependent via `_propagate_exclusions`. The user-facing diagnostic ("requires 'alphamod' 0.0.0 but the installed 'alphamod' is 1.0.0") reads as nonsense, since 1.0.0 is greater than 0.0.0. Fix is either to make the version key mandatory in a dependency entry or to default to `">=0.0.0"` rather than `"0.0.0"`.

findings.title: Case-colliding folder names: the codepoint-first folder is silently kept and the other refused, so folder name decides which mod loads
findings.failing_input: On a case-sensitive filesystem, two sibling folders whose names differ only in case, holding two UNRELATED mods: <root>/alphamod/mod.json declaring mod_id "alpha" and <root>/Alphamod/mod.json declaring mod_id "beta". candidate_folders returns sorted(["Alphamod","alphamod"]) = ["Alphamod", "alphamod"], so "Alphamod" is seen first, seen_folders.setdefault(key, name) records it (line 129), and only the SECOND folder gets parsed = None (line 128). Result: load_order == ['beta'], excluded == {'alpha': ['malformed_manifest']}. Now swap only the folder casing -- put mod "alpha" in Alphamod/ and mod "beta" in alphamod/ -- with byte-identical manifests, and the result flips to load_order == ['alpha'], excluded == {'beta': [...]}. I reproduced both outcomes by substituting discovery.candidate_folders with exactly the listing a Linux listdir would return.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the one place in Stage 4 where the folder name, not mod_id, decides semantic identity, and it fails OPEN: one of the two colliding folders is admitted into the live plan. It directly violates "folder name must NOT be able to alter semantic identity" and "must NEVER silently choose one duplicate/conflicting mod because it appeared first on disk" -- the winner here is just whichever name sorts first by codepoint, which is why flipping one letter's case flips which mod loads. discovery.py's own module docstring states the intended behaviour ("reports such a pair rather than silently depending on which platform is reading"), but the code resolves the ambiguity instead of refusing it. Contrast _index_by_id (resolve.py:99), which correctly drops BOTH claimants of a duplicate mod_id; the same fail-closed rule is missing here. Fix: on a collision, also mark the previously accepted entry's manifest as None and emit a diagnostic against it, e.g. keep a {key: index_in_found} map and retro-refuse the first entry.

findings.title: sorted() over a set that can contain None crashes the entire discovery scan
findings.failing_input: A mod "thief" declaring content ["Mod_thief_P"] whose container_reader returns package_paths = ["/Game/SurvivalGameKitV2/Foo", "/Game/Mods/victim/Meshes/SM_A"]. ns.owning_mod returns None for any path not under /Game/Mods/, so the set is {None, "victim"}; subtracting {"thief"} leaves {None, "victim"} and sorted() raises TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'NoneType'. The traceback goes manifest.check_artifacts -> discovery.discover (line 131, not wrapped in try) -> discovery.scan -> resolve.plan_from_root, so NO load plan is produced for ANY mod. Reproduced end-to-end. The single-element case is also wrong but silent: package_paths = ["/Game/Mods/thief/Meshes/SM_A", "/Game/SurvivalGameKitV2/Foo"] yields foreign == [None] and a CONTENT_NAMESPACE_MISMATCH reading "carries packages belonging to [None]".
findings.why_it_matters: Every other failure in Stage 4 is contained to the offending mod; this one takes down the whole pipeline with an unhandled TypeError, so a single mod shipping a container that references any non-/Game/Mods/ package path denies service to every other mod in the install. The test at tests/test_modframework.py:276 only ever feeds a single mod-owned foreign path, so the mixed case is untested. Fix: map the None bucket to a sentinel before sorting, e.g. foreign = sorted({ns.owning_mod(p) or "<not a mod path>" for p in ...} - {manifest.mod_id}), and decide deliberately whether a non-mod package path is a namespace mismatch or its own diagnostic.

findings.title: Cycle diagnostic prints the alphabetically sorted SCC as if it were the dependency chain, naming edges that do not exist
findings.failing_input: Three mods with edges aaa -> ccc, ccc -> bbb, bbb -> aaa. _strongly_connected returns the component already sorted (line 251), so component == ['aaa','bbb','ccc'] and the detail reads "is part of a dependency cycle: aaa -> bbb -> ccc -> aaa". aaa -> bbb and bbb -> ccc are not edges in either direction; the real chain is aaa -> ccc -> bbb -> aaa. Reproduced against the live resolver.
findings.why_it_matters: The diagnostic is the only thing a mod author has to act on, and it asserts a concrete dependency relationship that their manifests do not contain -- sending them to inspect aaa's dependency on bbb, which does not exist. The sorted component is the right thing to sort ON (it keeps the output deterministic) but it is not a traversal, so it must not be rendered with " -> ". Fix: either report the members as an unordered set ("members: aaa, bbb, ccc") or recover one real cycle by walking edges from component[0] within the component, which stays deterministic because edges[] is already sorted.

findings.title: A refused folder claiming another mod's mod_id evicts the real owner from the load plan
findings.failing_input: Three folders under one root: AlphaMod/mod.json = valid manifest_body("alphamod"); BetaMod/mod.json = valid, dependencies [{mod_id: alphamod, version: ^1.0.0}]; ZSquatter/mod.json = {"manifest_version":1,"mod_id":"alphamod","name":"x","version":"1.0.0","framework_api":"^9.0.0"} (refused for unsupported_framework_api, but parse() still returns declared_mod_id="alphamod"). Actual result from resolve.plan_from_root(root): load_order == [] and excluded == {"alphamod": ["unsupported_framework_api"], "betamod": ["dependency_excluded"]}. Expected: only the squatter refused, or at minimum a duplicate_mod_id naming both folders.
findings.why_it_matters: _index_by_id writes excluded[entry.identity] for every folder whose manifest was NOT accepted, and identity is the mod_id the folder merely CLAIMED. That key then collides with the accepted mod's real id: _check_cycles (line 262) drops it from the graph, _propagate_exclusions (line 294) sees 'alphamod' in excluded and kills every dependent, and _topological_order (line 318) computes live = set(accepted) - set(excluded), removing the healthy alphamod itself. So mod_id is NOT authoritative: an unrelated folder that never earned an identity gets to speak for one. It is a one-file denial of service against any mod (drop in a folder with a deliberately bad framework_api and the target plus its whole dependent subtree vanish), and the report actively misdirects - the only diagnostics are subject="alphamod" / "betamod"; the ZSquatter folder is never named anywhere in the plan, so a user is told alphamod requires framework API ^9.0.0 when the real alphamod requires ^0.4.0. Duplicate identity between an accepted mod and a refused claimant is exactly the ambiguity _index_by_id refuses to resolve for two accepted mods, yet here it is resolved silently against the innocent one.

findings.title: check_artifacts crashes with TypeError, aborting the entire scan, when a container mixes a non-mod path with a foreign mod path
findings.failing_input: EvilMod/mod.json declares content ["Mod_evilmod_P"], the three container files exist, and container_reader returns {"package_paths": ["/Game/SurvivalGameKitV2/Loot/DT_Items", "/Game/Mods/victim/Meshes/SM_Loot"]}. ns.owning_mod returns None for the first and "victim" for the second, so the expression evaluates sorted({None, "victim"} - {"evilmod"}) and raises: TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'NoneType'. Traceback: manifest.py:525 <- discovery.py:131 <- discovery.py:146 <- resolve.py:374.
findings.why_it_matters: The exception is not a Diagnostic and nothing catches it - the try/except a few lines above wraps only the container_reader call, so plan_from_root() dies and NO load plan and NO diagnostics are produced for any mod under the root. One hostile (or merely sloppy) container takes down discovery for the user's entire install, and it does so precisely inside the check that exists to stop a mod shipping another mod's package paths. The single-value case is also wrong in a quieter way: a container carrying only vanilla paths (e.g. /Game/SurvivalGameKitV2/Loot/DT_Items, which overwrites shipped game content) is reported as "carries packages belonging to [None]" - the one case where a mod is stamping on vanilla rather than on another mod is the case the message cannot name.

findings.title: Container stem is an unowned namespace: a mod may declare another mod's container stem and silently replace its container
findings.failing_input: AlphaMod/mod.json: content ["Mod_alphamod_P"] with those files in AlphaMod/Content. EvilMod/mod.json: content ["Mod_alphamod_P"] with EvilMod's OWN files under that same stem in EvilMod/Content, and a container_reader reporting only /Game/Mods/evilmod/... packages so the namespace cross-check passes. Actual result: load_order == ['alphamod', 'evilmod'], excluded == {}, diagnostics == [] (a completely clean plan), and staging_profile(plan) returns stage=[{src: AlphaMod/Content, stem: 'Mod_alphamod_P'}, {src: EvilMod/Content, stem: 'Mod_alphamod_P'}], expect=['Mod_alphamod_P', 'Mod_alphamod_P'].
findings.why_it_matters: manifest.check_artifacts (line 505) only verifies a stem's three files exist under the declaring mod's own folder; nothing binds the stem to mod_id (ns.container_name would give Mod_<mod_id>_P) and nothing in resolve.py compares stems across mods. runner/containers.apply_profile copies src/<stem>+suffix to stage_dir/<stem>+suffix in list order, so evilmod's .pak/.utoc/.ucas overwrite alphamod's at the same destination filenames - one mod's content answering for another's, which is the exact IoStore collision namespace.py's docstring says the derived paths exist to prevent. The downstream gate cannot catch it either: check_stage_dir does expected = sorted(set(expected)), collapsing the duplicate, so it reports consistent. containers_for(plan, 'evilmod') also returns ['Mod_alphamod_P'], so a selective unload of evilmod deletes alphamod's container.

findings.title: Case-colliding folder names: the first-sorted folder keeps its manifest, the second is refused
findings.failing_input: On a case-sensitive filesystem, two sibling folders 'MODX' (valid manifest, mod_id alphamod) and 'modx' (valid manifest, mod_id betamod). Reproduced by substituting discovery.candidate_folders to return [('MODX', p1), ('modx', p2)]: MODX comes back with mod_id=alphamod and no diagnostics, modx comes back with manifest=None and malformed_manifest, and resolve gives load_order ['alphamod'], excluded {'betamod': ['malformed_manifest']}.
findings.why_it_matters: Only the second occurrence has parsed set to None (line 128); the first was already accepted with its manifest intact. So the surviving mod is decided by the byte order of the folder NAME - rename 'MODX' to 'zmodx' and betamod loads instead of alphamod. That is the folder name altering which mod exists, which the framework's own comment at this site says it refuses to do ("Reported rather than resolved, because which of the two 'wins' would then depend on the platform"), and it violates the fail-closed rule that an ambiguous pair is refused rather than arbitrated. On Windows the pair is one folder and alphamod loads; on Linux both exist and betamod is dropped - the machine-dependent outcome the check was written to prevent.

findings.title: local_id is never validated, so expected_row_names publishes row names Stage 2 cannot own
findings.failing_input: EvilMod/Code/items.py returns [{'local_id': 'Loot__Rare', 'display_name': 'x', 'short_name': 'x', 'description': 'x', 'weight': 1.0, 'mesh': 'm', 'icon': 'i'}]. item_declarations() accepts it with zero diagnostics and expected_row_names() returns ['evilmod__Loot__Rare']; definition.ItemId.parse('evilmod__Loot__Rare') returns None, i.e. Stage 2 says that row belongs to no mod at all. Any non-string value (local_id: 42, local_id: {}) is accepted the same way - _validate_declaration only tests key presence and unknown keys, never a value.
findings.why_it_matters: manifest.py:382-388 goes out of its way to refuse a mod_id containing '__' because it makes the derived row name ambiguous to decompose - and then the other half of that same derived name is accepted unchecked. The row name is built at execution.py:191 by string interpolation rather than through ItemId, so Stage 4 hands the acceptance layer a row it asserts will appear in the game while registry.register (via ItemId/ItemDefinition) can never create it, and misclassifies it as ERR_COLLIDES_WITH_VANILLA if a row by that name is already present. A plan Stage 4 declared clean therefore fails at registration time, which is the failure this stage exists to move earlier, and the mod_id Stage 4 correctly attaches at line 124 is defeated by the unvalidated half of the pair.

findings.title: A refused duplicate loses its declared mod_id, so the other claimant silently loads and duplicate_mod_id is never raised
findings.why_it_matters: parse() returns `None, out, None` as the third value even though `raw.get("mod_id")` is present and would pass ns.check_mod_id -- contradicting the function's own docstring ("The third value is what the file CLAIMED to be, and it is returned even when the manifest is refused"). Discovered.identity (discovery.py:66) therefore falls back to the folder path, and resolve._index_by_id (resolve.py:91) files the exclusion under that path instead of under 'lib'. The mod_id 'lib' is claimed by two folders and one of them is silently chosen -- exactly what the duplicate rule forbids. It is also unstable: the day the framework starts supporting manifest_version 99, the SAME tree flips from load_order ['lib'] to both copies refused. The same root cause misreports dependents: with only the manifest_version:99 copy of lib installed, a mod requiring it gets `missing_dependency` ("not present in the load set", i.e. go download it) instead of `dependency_excluded`, which is the exact distinction resolve.py:120-129 was written to make.

findings.title: Duplicate mod_id is counted only over manifests that fully validated, so a duplicate paired with any other failure is never detected
findings.failing_input:
Mods/GoodLib/mod.json  -> mod_id "lib", version 1.0.0, framework_api "^0.4.0"   (valid)
Mods/EvilLib/mod.json  -> mod_id "lib", version 2.0.0, framework_api "^9.0.0"   (refused)
Mods/App/mod.json      -> mod_id "app", dependencies [{mod_id:"lib", version:"^1.0.0"}]
resolve.plan_from_root(root) gives:
  diagnostics codes == ['dependency_excluded', 'unsupported_framework_api']
  excluded == {'lib': ['unsupported_framework_api'], 'app': ['dependency_excluded']}
  D.DUPLICATE_MOD_ID appears nowhere.
findings.why_it_matters: `by_id` is only populated from entries where `entry.manifest is not None`, so a folder that claims an id but fails any other check never counts as a claimant. duplicate_mod_id is one of the nine failure classes Stage 4 must detect, and here two folders claim one authoritative identity with zero mention of it. The report is actively misleading: the perfectly valid GoodLib is dropped (accepted['lib'] collides with excluded['lib'] so live == {}) and the user is told 'lib' was refused for unsupported_framework_api -- a fact about a folder they were never shown. Note this case only fails closed by accident of the key collision; combined with finding #1 (where the key does not collide) the same gap becomes an outright leak into load_order.

findings.title: A case-insensitive folder collision refuses only the second folder; the first survives purely because its name sorts earlier
findings.failing_input:
On a case-sensitive filesystem, two mod folders whose names collide under lower():
  Mods/ModA/mod.json -> mod_id "alphamod"
  Mods/moda/mod.json -> mod_id "betamod"
candidate_folders sorts to ('ModA','moda') ('M'=0x4D < 'm'=0x6D), so:
  load_order == ['alphamod'], excluded == {'betamod': ['malformed_manifest']}
Rename the pair to modA/ and moda/ (nothing else changed) and the survivor flips:
  load_order == ['betamod'], excluded == {'alphamod': ['malformed_manifest']}
(Reproduced by monkeypatching discovery.candidate_folders to return the colliding pair, which is what a case-sensitive fs hands back.)
findings.why_it_matters: The inline comment two lines above claims the pair is 'Reported rather than resolved, because which of the two "wins" would then depend on the platform reading the directory' -- but the code does resolve it, keeping whichever folder name sorts first. That is the ambiguity the requirement forbids resolving, and it makes a folder rename semantic rather than cosmetic: renaming ModA to modA moves a different mod_id into the load plan. Fail-closed here means refusing both sides of the collision. Secondary: the surviving-side exclusion is filed under the loser's mod_id with code malformed_manifest, so the user reads 'betamod: malformed_manifest' for a mod whose manifest parsed cleanly.

findings.title: A mod whose code emits a fatally invalid declaration still contributes its other declarations to the live execution plan
findings.failing_input:
Mods/PartialMod/mod.json -> mod_id "partial", code: ["items.py"]
Mods/PartialMod/Code/items.py:
  def item_definitions():
      return [
        {"local_id":"good", "display_name":"Good", "short_name":"good",
         "description":"fine", "weight":1.0, "mesh":"m", "icon":"i"},
        {"mod_id":"othermod", "local_id":"stolen", "display_name":"Stolen",
         "short_name":"stolen", "description":"...", "weight":1.0,
         "mesh":"m", "icon":"i"},
      ]
resolve.plan_from_root(root) -> load_order ['partial'], excluded {}
execution.item_declarations(plan) -> declarations [{'local_id':'good', 'mod_id':'partial'}]
                                   + a FATAL malformed_manifest diagnostic against 'partial'
execution.expected_row_names(...) -> ['partial__good']
findings.why_it_matters: diagnostics.py:13-19 defines fatal as 'removes its subject from the load plan ... never loads "the good part" of a mod whose manifest it could not fully accept', and discovery.py:130-137 enforces exactly that for artifacts. execution.py does not: `_validate_declaration` returns None for the illegal entry, the loop skips it, and the mod's remaining rows are handed to the live registration layer while the mod stays in load_order with its containers staged. So a mod caught attempting to register into another mod's namespace is still partially loaded. The same partial acceptance occurs when a mod ships two code artifacts and one raises on import (execution.py:147-152 `continue`) -- the surviving file's items are still registered. The acceptance check at research/instruments/mods/stage4_acceptance.py:268-271 cannot catch this: it only asserts {d['mod_id'] for d in declarations} - set(plan.load_order) is empty, which holds here.
